summary: Describes the User-based Security Model for SNMP version 3, giving message-level security with authentication and privacy. It includes a MIB for managing the model's configuration. It replaces RFC 2264 and was replaced by RFC 2574.

eli5.summary: It signs and seals network-manager messages so only the right people can send and read them. This is an update of an earlier version that was itself replaced.

questions: what is the snmpv3 user-based security model
what is the usm time window
what is key localization in snmp
subtitle: How SNMPv3 signs and optionally encrypts management messages using users, shared secrets and a 150-second timeliness window.

tldr.problem: SNMP management messages can be altered, forged by someone pretending to be another user, or replayed later. A security model needs to stop that without depending on other services such as NTP or a key management protocol.
tldr.mechanism: The User-based Security Model (USM) ties security to named users with secret keys. It authenticates the whole message with HMAC-MD5-96 or HMAC-SHA-96, optionally encrypts the payload with CBC-DES, and rejects messages outside a 150-second window based on the authoritative engine's boot count and clock.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2274 is a Proposed Standard that replaced RFC 2264 to correct a clerical error in the module number assignment, and it was itself replaced by RFC 2574.

today: RFC 2274 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 2574, so current work should follow that document. It replaced RFC 2264, which carried a clerical error in the snmpModules number assignment.

sections.title: Threats, Goals and Module Layout
sections.content:
USM fits into the SNMP architecture of RFC 2271 as a security model, and its main idea is the traditional concept of a user identified by a userName. The principal threats are modification of information and masquerade. Disclosure and message stream modification are secondary threats with limited protection. Denial of service and traffic analysis are explicitly out of scope.

The goals are to verify that a message was not modified, to verify the user's identity, to detect messages that were not recently generated, and when necessary to hide contents. Two design constraints are that effective management during network stress is preferred over security where they conflict, and that the mechanism must not depend on services such as NTP or key management protocols.

The model is split into an authentication module, a fixed timeliness module and a privacy module. HMAC-MD5-96 MUST be supported, HMAC-SHA-96 SHOULD be supported, and CBC-DES privacy is optional. Privacy requires authentication, and the RFC notes that none of the three services can be had alone in the way one might expect: integrity and origin authentication come together, and confidentiality needs both.
sections.eli5: The goal is to stop people from changing, faking or replaying the notes sent to a network device, while keeping things simple enough to work when the network is having a bad day.

sections.title: Users, Engines and Replay Protection
sections.content:
Each user has a userName, a securityName, an authentication protocol and key (authKey), and a privacy protocol and key (privKey). The keys are not accessible via SNMP and normally differ at each authoritative engine. They can be changed remotely only with the key change objects.

One engine in each exchange is authoritative: the receiver when the message expects a response (Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set, Inform), and the sender when it does not (SNMPv2-Trap, Response, Report). Each engine keeps snmpEngineID, snmpEngineBoots (reboot count, stored in non-volatile memory) and snmpEngineTime (seconds since the last boots increment). This means no clock that ticks while powered off is needed.

The Time Window is 150 seconds for all users. An authenticated message is rejected as notInTimeWindow if its boots value differs from the authoritative engine's, if its time differs by more than 150 seconds, or if snmpEngineBoots has latched at 2147483647. A non-authoritative engine learns and caches the remote values from authenticated messages, so no separate synchronization step is needed.
sections.eli5: One side is the boss clock. Messages carry the boss's boot count and time, and anything more than about two and a half minutes old is thrown away, like a ticket that has expired.

sections.title: The Security Parameters Field
sections.content:
USM puts its data in the msgSecurityParameters field, an OCTET STRING holding a BER-encoded sequence. It carries six values: msgAuthoritativeEngineID, msgAuthoritativeEngineBoots and msgAuthoritativeEngineTime (both 0 to 2147483647), msgUserName (1 to 32 octets), msgAuthenticationParameters and msgPrivacyParameters.

The last two are defined by whichever authentication and privacy protocols the user has. When a feature is not used, the field holds the NULL string.
sections.eli5: Every message has a small label on it saying whose boss clock it uses, what time that clock showed, who sent it, and the seal and lock details.

sections.title: Sending, Receiving and Discovery
sections.content:
When sending, the engine looks up the user, encrypts the scoped PDU if privacy is requested, fills in the engine ID, boots, time and user name, then authenticates the whole message. A Request may use an empty engine ID and zero boots and time.

When receiving, the engine checks in order: parse of the security parameters, known engine ID, known user name, supported security level, the authentication check, the time window, and finally decryption. Each failure increments a specific counter such as usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs, usmStatsUnknownUserNames, usmStatsUnsupportedSecLevels, usmStatsWrongDigests, usmStatsNotInTimeWindows or usmStatsDecryptionErrors, and the counter is returned so a Report PDU can be built.

Discovery lets a non-authoritative engine learn what it needs. It sends a noAuthNoPriv request with user name initial, a zero-length engine ID and an empty variable binding list. The Report that comes back carries the engine ID and the usmStatsUnknownEngineIDs counter. For authenticated communication, a second authenticated request with boots and time of zero yields a Report with the current values and usmStatsNotInTimeWindows.
sections.eli5: A new manager first asks, who are you, and learns the device's ID and clock from the answer. Then each message goes through a checklist, and if any step fails a tally counter is bumped.

sections.title: Authentication, Privacy and Keys
sections.content:
HMAC-MD5-96 uses a 16-octet key and HMAC-SHA-96 a 20-octet key. Both compute an HMAC over the whole message and carry only the first 12 octets (96 bits) in msgAuthenticationParameters. While computing, the field holds 12 zero octets. The key is padded to 64 octets and XORed with 0x36 and 0x5C to make K1 and K2.

CBC-DES encrypts the scoped PDU. The first 8 octets of the 16-octet privacy key are the DES key, and the last 8 are a pre-IV that is XORed with an 8-octet salt built from the engine's 32-bit boots value and a local 32-bit integer. The salt goes in msgPrivacyParameters so the receiver can decrypt. Data is padded to a multiple of 8 octets.

Key localization lets a person keep one password. The password becomes a key Ku, and the localized key for an engine is a hash of Ku, the engine's ID and Ku again. A compromise of one device's key then does not reveal the password or the keys for other engines.
sections.eli5: The seal is made by mixing the message with a secret and keeping a short fingerprint. The lock scrambles the contents in blocks. One password makes a different key for each device, so losing one key does not open every door.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Conformance
sections.content:
Recommended practices include discarding Responses that match no outstanding Request, using different msgIDs and request-ids within each 150-second window, and doing time synchronization with authenticated messages. Because an authenticated message can be replayed during its window, Set operations should wait for acknowledgement, and snmpSetSerialNo from RFC 1907 can enforce ordering.

Passwords must be at least 8 characters if the Appendix A algorithm is used. Using the same password for authentication and privacy is called very poor practice. A user's password or non-localized key MUST NOT be stored on a managed device; only the localized key SHALL be stored.

To be a Secure SNMP implementation an engine MUST implement an authentication protocol, protect users' secrets, implement key localization and implement the SNMP-USER-BASED-SM-MIB. A privacy protocol is optional.
sections.eli5: Do not reuse the same secret for two jobs, pick a hard password, and never keep the master password on the device itself. Only keep the device's own copy of the key.
